description: The deterministic projection from the selected XNA contract to Common Lisp. tools/api-compat/verify.py applies these rules to the live image; docs/common-lisp-mapping.md is the prose that explains them.

naming.identifier: A CLR identifier becomes a Lisp symbol by inserting a hyphen at each case boundary and lowercasing. Texture2D becomes texture-2d, because the D after the digit starts a new word; Bgra4444 becomes bgra4444, because nothing does. That is the same rule the generated ABI constants already follow.
naming.reference_type_member: <member>, in the type's package, as a generic function or reader.
naming.value_type_member: <type>-<member>, in the type's package. The prefix is what keeps Rectangle's Left from colliding with Viewport's.
naming.static_class_member: <class>-<member>, so that Mouse and GamePad can join Keyboard's namespace without collision.
naming.constructor: make-instance for a reference type; make-<type> for a value type.
naming.enum_member: a keyword named by the identifier rule; the exact value is preserved in the runtime table.

Components.reason: The game's one collection, answered by identity because XNA's is a field.

LaunchParameters.reason: Answered by identity, as XNA's field is. CNA has no route that reports a game's launch parameters, so it is empty unless the program fills it -- recorded in docs/limitations.md rather than left to be discovered.

Content.reason: The game's own content manager, answered by identity because XNA's is a field. Read-only, and the missing setter is deliberate: XNA's Game.Content = m assigns a reference, and CNA's cna_game_set_content_manager_ext *copies* -- its own header says "the canonical setter takes a reference and copies, so this does too: the caller keeps its own manager". Reading the property back would therefore answer a different object than the one assigned, so the member is reported partial rather than projected as something that silently means something else. docs/limitations.md.

Window.reason: Game.Window over the GameWindow facade, answering the same object every time as XNA's property does. Get-only, as XNA's is.

unimplemented.ShowMissingRequirementMessage(Exception): A **protected** virtual (`.method family` in the pinned Game assembly), and one of the raiser-shaped family rather than a member of its own. XNA calls it from inside `Run`'s two catch handlers -- for NoSuitableGraphicsDeviceException and NoAudioHardwareException -- and *rethrows when it answers false*. CNA runs the loop and catches nothing into Lisp: measured against 0.21.0, CNA_GameCallbacks and CNA_GameFrameHooks have load_content, update, draw, unload_content, exiting, initialize, begin_run, end_run, begin_draw and end_draw, and no hook for a run that failed to start. So an override here would never be called. The reason that used to stand said it needed "the CLR exception projection and a platform message box". **CNA has a message box** -- cna_message_box_show_ext and cna_message_box_get_is_supported_ext -- so that half was wrong, and the half that actually blocks it went unmentioned. Its dispatch is also entirely `isinst` on those two exception types, and neither is in the selection.
unimplemented.Services: GameServiceContainer, which CNA does not have a container for. Activated.reason: A CLR event is two operations, add_E and remove_E, and it projects to two generic functions on the object that raises it. The handler takes the sender and nothing else: EventArgs.Empty carries no information, and a second always-empty argument would be something every handler had to write and ignore.

Load(String).reason: Load<T> is generic over the asset type, and this is the one place the projection is closer to XNA than the C ABI can be: CNA spells the generic method as one route per asset type -- because a C caller cannot name a type. Common Lisp can, so the type stays an argument and Load<T> stays one member. LOADABLE-ASSET-TYPES answers which types have a route. **Four of them do**, and the four are the ones the selection has: cna_content_manager_load_texture2d, _load_texture_cube, _load_sprite_font and, in effects.h rather than content.h, cna_content_manager_load_effect -- which CNA's header calls "the canonical Load<Effect> specialization, which is the route an XNA game's ContentManager.Load<Effect> takes". It reads a compiled .xnb Effect asset, a .cnj descriptor naming a stock effect, and a .cnj descriptor carrying shader source; only the compiled shape needs CNA_GRAPHICS_CAPABILITY_COMPILED_EFFECTS, so the descriptor shapes load on both qualification renderers and are tested there. Reported partial because Load<T> is generic over *any* type with a content reader and this is four. CNA also has _load_sound_effect and _load_model, whose types are not in the selection, and _load_foreign_ext and _load_object_dictionary_ext, which are extensions rather than Load<T>. The reason that used to stand named three routes and called them "the ones CNA has a route for", which was wrong by one -- and the one it missed was for a type this binding already projects. **And one asset type cannot be offered on one admitted ABI at all.** On CNA 0.21.0 `cna_model_destroy' applied to a model that came from `cna_content_manager_load_model' is a null dereference at offset 0x490, so a loaded model could never be released; it is fixed in 0.22.0, and both were measured with the same fixture. There is no sound fallback -- leaking the handle would give a game that cannot shut down instead of a crash -- so `Load<Model>' refuses on 0.21.0, before anything is created, and names the defect. The other five asset types load on both.

Unload().reason: Read from the pinned IL: Unload throws ObjectDisposedException when loadedAssets is already null, walks disposableAssets calling IDisposable.Dispose on every entry, and clears both collections in a finally. All three are reproduced. The manager keeps XNA's two collections -- a name-keyed cache and a disposal list -- so it has assets of its own to release, and Unload releases them: a SpriteFont before the atlas it keeps alive, and a later asset before an earlier one. CNA's cna_content_manager_unload is called as well, so neither side is left holding an asset the other has let go. **One deliberate divergence, and it is documented:** XNA's Unload has no error handling, so a throwing Dispose stops it while the finally still clears both collections -- which strands every remaining asset with nothing left that can reach it. There are no finalizers here by policy, so reproducing that would leak permanently and fail the game's teardown; this releases every independent asset and then signals the first failure. docs/limitations.md.

Dispose().reason: XNA's Dispose() is Dispose(true) followed by GC.SuppressFinalize, and Dispose(bool) is Unload() and then nulling both collections -- a purely managed operation that destroys nothing native. That is what happens here, for **both** kinds of manager. A game's own manager is disposable: it unloads its assets and is marked disposed, and the borrowed native manager CNA says "cannot be destroyed" is left alone, which is no loss because XNA has nothing native to destroy either. Game.Content keeps answering the disposed manager afterwards, as XNA's field does, and every member on it then refuses -- ObjectDisposedException on that side, CNA-DISPOSED-ERROR on this one. A manager this binding created additionally destroys its native object, which is the one thing XNA has no counterpart for because it has no native object.

.ctor.reason: XNA tells the integer and float constructors apart by static type, and Common Lisp would have to tell 1 from 1.0 at run time to do the same. Those two mean almost opposite colours -- (make-color 1 1 1) is very nearly black where (make-color-from-floats 1.0 1.0 1.0) is white -- so the distinction is a name here rather than a numeric type nobody can see. The Vector3 and Vector4 forms are named for the same reason, and their arity would not separate them anyway.

FromNonPremultiplied.reason: The two overloads are different computations, not one operation reached two ways: the integer form truncates an integer quotient and the Vector4 form multiplies in floats and packs through PackUNorm. They disagree by a level on ordinary inputs, so collapsing them would hide a real difference.

FromStream(GraphicsDevice,Stream).reason: **Partial, and the fit is why.** Read from the assembly, this overload is the five-argument private constructor called with the graphics profile's MaxTextureSize for both extents and image operation 0 -- so XNA caps an oversized image at what the profile can hold. Those extents are readable: ProfileCapabilities.MaxTextureSize is 0x800 for Reach and 0x1000 for HiDef, hardcoded in the pinned assembly, and GraphicsProfile is projected. What stops it is what the fit *does*. XNA's happens inside UnsafeNativeMethods::DecodeStreamToTexture, a P/Invoke into unmanaged code the pinned assembly does not contain -- the extents go in by reference and come back rewritten -- so the pinned authority does not say whether operation 0 enlarges an image smaller than the box. CNA's does: measured against 0.21.0, a decode info with zoom false **scales in both directions**. A 16x8 PNG fitted into 64x64 comes back 64x32, and into 4x4 comes back 4x2. So passing MaxTextureSize here would return a 2048x2048 texture for an 8x8 PNG, which is not what this member means. A null decode info "preserves source dimensions", which is this overload without the cap, and that is what it does: an image within the profile's limit decodes identically, and one larger than it decodes at its own size here and at the limit there. The reason that used to stand said "ABI 0.21.0 reports no maximum texture size for the fit to be computed from -- GraphicsProfile and the whole device-capability surface are themselves missing". Both halves were wrong: cna_graphics_device_get_renderer_limit_ext answers CNA_RENDERER_LIMIT_MAX_TEXTURE_DIMENSION, CNA_RendererInfo carries max_texture_dimension, and GraphicsProfile has been complete since the device-settings closure. Neither is the number XNA uses anyway, which is the profile constant above.

frontier_category_kinds.LANGUAGE_PROJECTION_LIMIT: The Common Lisp projection cannot express the member, or the type it needs has no counterpart a Lisp program could use safely. IntPtr is the standing example: the number sometimes exists and a bare integer is not a pointer type. Changing this needs a decision about the public API, not a CNA release.
frontier_category_kinds.CNA_ADMITTED_ABI_LIMIT: No admitted CNA ABI can represent the member. At least one of the versions in the admitted set has no route for it, or its route cannot express what the member means. The category names the compatibility policy rather than a version, because the admitted set is a set -- a member that only one admitted version could express is as unrepresentable as one no version can, since the binding promises the same public surface against every version it admits. Includes every protected On<Event> raiser, because CNA raises the event itself and offers no hook to stand in front of it. Changing this needs a CNA release and a re-qualification, and each entry names the route it read -- concrete per-version evidence such as "0.21.0 lacks route X" stays in the entry, where it is a fact, rather than in the category name, where it was a policy. This category was called CNA_0_21_ABI_LIMIT while exactly one version was admitted.
frontier_category_kinds.PUBLIC_OBJECT_MODEL_CLOSURE: Implementable against every admitted CNA ABI, but only as a new closure in this binding's object model rather than as a member. The owned GraphicsDevice is the standing example: the routes exist and supporting them means a second kind of device beside the parent-owned facade. This read "implementable against 0.21.0" while exactly one version was admitted.
frontier_category_kinds.DEPENDENCY_NOT_SELECTED: Blocked on a type that is not in the selected profile. Resolved by selecting that type, which is a profile decision.
frontier_category_kinds.QUALIFICATION_LIMIT: Implemented, but some part of it cannot be evidenced, so it is not claimed complete. Not a missing capability: a missing proof.
frontier_category_kinds.IMPLEMENTABLE_BUT_LOW_VALUE: Nothing blocks it and it is not worth the surface. No member is in this category; it exists so that a future one has somewhere honest to go.
frontier_category_kinds.IMPLEMENTABLE_AND_HIGH_VALUE: Nothing blocks it and it should be done next. **Empty is the point**: an entry here is a to-do the scoreboard is hiding, and three members sat in this state behind wrong reasons until the route-by-route audit found them.

frontier_categories_description: One category per non-complete selected member, keyed by '<type>.<signature>' exactly as the generated report names it. Every missing and partial member must appear here and nothing else may: verify.py reports an uncategorised_absence otherwise, so a member cannot go non-complete without saying what kind of thing is stopping it. The prose reason stays where it was -- per member in 'unimplemented' and in 'member_overrides' -- because a reason names a route and a category sorts it. See 'frontier_category_kinds'.
